description: A dramatic, real-world timeline of how DoorDash scaled while Uber Eats and Grubhub fought for survival during the on-demand delivery boom (and the margin squeeze that followed).
youtube_description:
🚚 Chapter Race: DoorDash’s delivery dominance vs. Uber Eats—and Grubhub’s exit.

00:00 — The early delivery boom (2017–2018)
DoorDash grows quickly from 90M orders (2017) to 130M (2018), while Uber Eats climbs from 60M to 95M—setting up a head-to-head market for “fast enough” food.

01:05 — 2019: scale accelerates
DoorDash hits 190M orders in 2019; Uber Eats reaches 140M. The chart race starts to feel inevitable: restaurants want more demand, and platforms want more density.

02:10 — 2020: pandemic tailwind (the inflection year)
Orders explode. DoorDash jumps to 400M (2020). Uber Eats surges to 260M. This is where the leaders lock in habits—and where logistics math starts favoring the biggest networks.

03:15 — 2021: the peak expansion
DoorDash rises to 560M (2021). Uber Eats tops out around 320M. Growth is still strong, but the margins battle begins behind the scenes.

04:20 — 2022–2023: the squeeze
DoorDash reaches 610M (2022) then 680M (2023). Uber Eats slows—300M (2022) to 280M (2023). Grubhub collapses from 30M (2022) to 15M (2023).

05:10 — 2024–2026: consolidation completes the story
Grubhub hits 0 by 2024 as the delivery landscape consolidates. DoorDash keeps pulling away: 740M (2024), 780M (2025), 820M (2026). Uber Eats stabilizes and climbs modestly to 325M by 2026.

👉 Watch the race, then comment: Which part of this chart race matters more—customer habit (repeat orders) or unit economics (delivery margins)?

Like/Subscribe for more chart-race timelines.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The delivery chart race where one app kept winning while another got squeezed.

In 2017, DoorDash was already pulling serious demand—about 90M orders—while Uber Eats sat around 60M and Grubhub hovered at ~35M. Back then, on-demand delivery felt like a “nice-to-have.” But the real story starts when density (more orders in the same neighborhoods) turns into an advantage.

By 2019, DoorDash jumped to 190M orders, turning local restaurant partnerships into a national machine. Uber Eats followed to ~140M, closing the gap—but not enough. Then 2020 hit, and the world changed overnight: DoorDash rocketed to 400M orders, while Uber Eats surged to 260M. The pandemic didn’t just increase demand—it trained customers to order on apps like a habit.

2021 is where the winner’s silhouette gets sharp. DoorDash climbs to ~560M orders, and Uber Eats reaches its peak around ~320M. But the “delivery boom” wasn’t pure growth—costs were rising too. Customers became less tolerant of fees, and platforms faced a brutal tradeoff: push orders through promotions, or protect margins and risk churn.

Then 2022–2023 tells the drama. DoorDash holds strong at 610M (2022) and 680M (2023). Uber Eats softens from ~300M to ~280M. Meanwhile, Grubhub collapses from ~30M (2022) to ~15M (2023), and by 2024 the chart goes to 0—consolidation completed, and the platform story ended.

Fast-forward: DoorDash keeps expanding—740M (2024) → 780M (2025) → an estimated 820M (2026). Uber Eats stabilizes and lifts to ~325M by 2026.

So here’s the question: in a delivery race like this, what wins more—repeat customer habit, or winning unit economics?
